title: The pieces: schemes, principals and policies
summary: What AddAuthentication, AddJwtBearer and TokenValidationParameters do, and the ClaimsPrincipal that comes out of them.

steps.title: How a real app wires it up
body: In production you don't hand-write token validation. With the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer` package an API looks like this:
app.UseAuthentication();   // reads the token, sets HttpContext.User
- An **authentication scheme** is a named handler that turns a request into an identity ("Bearer", "Cookies").
- **`UseAuthentication`** runs the default scheme on every request and puts the result in `HttpContext.User`. A missing token is not an error; the user is just anonymous.
- **`UseAuthorization`** looks at the endpoint's requirements and either lets it run, **challenges** (`401`, not authenticated) or **forbids** (`403`, authenticated but not allowed).
Everything in the JWT module maps onto these options. The sandbox has no NuGet, so in this module you build the same pieces from the framework's own building blocks.

steps.title: ClaimsPrincipal
body: Whatever the scheme, the result is a `System.Security.Claims.ClaimsPrincipal`:
- An identity created **without** an `authenticationType` has `IsAuthenticated == false`, even with claims. That's the anonymous user ASP.NET gives you by default.

- `IsInRole` checks claims of the identity's `roleType`. By default that's the long `ClaimTypes.Role` URI, not `"role"`, which is why JWT apps either pass `roleType: "role"` or turn off claim mapping.

code: var claims = new[] { new Claim("sub", "ada"), new Claim("role", "editor") };
steps.explain: No authentication type means not authenticated. And the first identity uses the default role claim type, so a claim literally named `role` doesn't count as a role there.

steps.prompt: Arrange the startup code of an API that uses authorization.
steps.explain: Services before `Build()`. Authentication must run before authorization, because authorization needs to know who the user is.

steps.prompt: An API calls `user.IsInRole("admin")` and it is always `false`, although the token clearly has `"role": "admin"`. The most likely cause?
options: The identity's role claim type is the default `ClaimTypes.Role` URI, not `"role"`
`IsInRole` is case-insensitive and found two roles
steps.explain: Pass `roleType: "role"` when building the identity (or set `RoleClaimType` in `TokenValidationParameters`, or disable inbound claim mapping).

steps.prompt: Build an authenticated identity whose name and roles come from JWT claims.

steps.title: From payload to principal
prompt: Write `ClaimsPrincipal ToPrincipal(string payloadJson)` that turns a (validated) JWT payload into a principal:
- one `Claim` per property, with the property name as type and the value's `ToString()` as value (`"exp": 2000` becomes `"2000"`),
- an array becomes **one claim per element** (`"role": ["admin", "user"]` gives two `role` claims),
- the identity has authentication type `"Bearer"`, name type `"sub"`, role type `"role"`.
solution: foreach (var item in prop.Value.EnumerateArray()) claims.Add(new Claim(prop.Name, item.ToString()));
template: Dojo.Eq("scope is one claim", "tasks:read tasks:write", dojoU.FindFirst("scope")?.Value);
Dojo.Eq("a single string role works too", true, ToPrincipal("{\"sub\":\"bob\",\"role\":\"editor\"}").IsInRole("editor"));
